extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, literary critics, poets, and philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for evaluating and producing poetry, allegory, and tragedy within an aesthetic theory that treats art as revelation of Ideas (objectifications of the will). Emphasises appropriate medium, form-specific aims, technical means (epithets, rhythm, metaphor), unity/plausibility, and the nature and purpose of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of allegory to the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory has an entirely different relation to poetry from that which it has to plastic and pictorial art; in the latter it leads away from what is perceptibly given and is to be rejected, but in poetry it is permissible and very serviceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In plastic and pictorial art allegory distracts from perception (the proper object of those arts), whereas in poetry the conception is the given and may be used to call up perceptions in the hearer’s imagination. Pictorial allegory that merely serves poetical meaning should be regarded as symbol or emblem and judged as poetic, not pictorial, worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of art: revelation of the Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of art is the revelation of the Ideas, the grades of the objectification of will, and the communication of them to the hearer with distinctness and vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas are essentially perceptible and can only be known by perception; art should produce perceptible representatives of abstract conceptions so the spectator/hearer apprehends the Idea. The artist’s skill is likened to a chemist who precipitates the concrete out of abstract universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s material and method: arrange conceptions to precipitate the perceptible
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry the abstract conceptions are the immediate material and must be so arranged that their spheres intersect each other to produce a perceptible representative for the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet narrows universality through combination and selection so the imagination can perceive the Idea; the 'precipitate' of the concrete must be obtained by the manner in which concepts are combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tropes (simile, metaphor, parable, allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes, metaphors, parables, and allegories are means by which abstract conceptions are made perceptible in language-arts; they differ in length and completeness of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices are of striking effect in poetry: e.g., Cervantes’ sleep as 'a mantle that covers all mankind', Homer’s description of Ate, Menenius Agrippa’s fable. Use them to make abstract thought vivid through concrete example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary symbolism (symbols becoming 'dumb')
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is merely an arbitrary connection between what is presented to perception and its abstract significance, allegory passes into symbol, which rests on agreement and can in time lose meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols risk becoming unintelligible when their conventional meaning is forgotten (e.g., the fish as Christian symbol). Ensure symbolic connections are intelligible and not purely arbitrary if the work is to remain communicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epithets and adjectival narrowing as a technical aid
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous epithets in poetry serve to narrow the universality of a concept until a perceptible image is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach qualifying adjectives to substantives so their conceptual sphere is intersected and made nearer to perception (illustrated by Homer’s frequent adjectival usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and rhyme as perceptual and persuasive aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm and rhyme hold attention and produce a kind of 'blind consent' to what is read, giving the poem an emphatic power of convincing independent of reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regular sound patterns because our faculties of perception have a temporal quality that follows recurring sounds; rhythm/rhyme both sustain attention and predispose acceptance prior to judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form matters: choose descriptive, narrative, or dramatic mode appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry can be descriptive, narrative, or directly dramatic depending on the Ideas to be represented; different grades of objectivity call for different poetic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower grades of objectified will may be better served by plastic art, whereas man (with actions, thoughts, emotions) suits poetry, especially forms that can represent progression (epic, drama). Select form according to the Idea’s grade and the nature of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs history: aim for inner/universal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet comprehends the Idea (the inner nature of man) apart from relations and time, whereas the historian apprehends phenomena in their relations and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For knowledge of man’s inner nature prefer poetic representation which gives a higher degree of 'inner truth'; historians are constrained by data and the principle of sufficient reason and thus present the phenomenon rather than the Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric-specific criterion: expression of will-subjectivity and alternation with pure knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The lyric is the subject of will (the singer’s volition) experienced as emotion (joy or grief) and alternates with moments of pure, will-less knowing; this mingled state is the essence of the lyric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true lyric should capture the interplay of desire (personal ends) and fleeting contemplative perception; lyrical works often reflect universal human situations despite being momentary impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of objectivity across poetic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic forms exhibit varying degrees of objectivity: ballad (some subjectivity), idyll (less), romantic poem (still less), epic (almost none), drama (most objective and most difficult).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the poet’s intended degree of objectivity to the form: lyrical is easiest and more subjective, drama requires the greatest objectivity and complexity of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by significant characters and pregnant situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The revelation of the Idea of man is principally attained by faithful representation of significant characters and by inventing 'pregnant' situations in which their qualities fully unfold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select characters and situations that bring out peculiar qualities in sharp outline; arrange and select so accidental or irrelevant elements are omitted. Unity, truthfulness to human nature, and significance of situations are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, plausibility, and avoidance of contradiction or impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute truth (inner truth) and unity are necessary conditions of poetic effect; contradictions of character, impossibility, or very great improbability in events offend as much as bad technique in painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters remain consistent with themselves and human nature; avoid improbable or impossible occurrences even in accessories. Faults here undermine the poetic 'mirror of life'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and proper treatment of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the summit of poetical art whose end is the representation of the terrible side of life—unspeakable pain, triumph of evil, scornful mastery of chance, and irretrievable fall of the innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must present great misfortune; this may be introduced by (1) a character of extraordinary wickedness, (2) blind fate (chance/error), or (3) the position of dramatis personæ relative to one another (ordinary characters compelled by relations). The third type is preferred for bringing misfortune near and showing it as arising naturally from human relations. Tragedy culminates in knowledge that may produce resignation or surrender of the will; demands for 'poetical justice' misunderstand tragedy’s nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical transparency: open/avowed vs concealed allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical works may be openly avowed (explicit allegory) or be concealed allegories in which deeper meanings are wrapped in narrative or satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: open - Balthasar Gracian’s Criticon; concealed - Don Quixote and Gulliver’s Travels. Recognize both modes and judge by how effectively the allegory renders the Idea perceptible rather than by mere surface symbolism.
